pharm-micro:bactmap.q: Which class inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit?

A 21-year-old student has 2 weeks of low-grade fever, dry cough and malaise; chest X-ray shows patchy interstitial infiltrates and cold agglutinin titers are elevated. The causative organism has no cell wall. Which antibiotic class would be ineffective?
pharm-micro:bactmap.e: Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks peptidoglycan, so cell-wall inhibitors have no target. Ribosomal (macrolide, tetracycline) and gyrase inhibitors remain active.

pharm-micro:penicillin.q: Penicillinase-resistant penicillins (nafcillin, dicloxacillin) are used for:

A 24-year-old man has a painless, indurated genital ulcer with a clean base and nontender inguinal lymphadenopathy for 1 week. Dark-field microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows motile spirochetes. Most appropriate treatment?
o: Benzathine penicillin G, single IM dose
pharm-micro:penicillin.e: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) is treated with IM benzathine penicillin G. Acyclovir treats HSV, whose ulcers are painful and vesicular.

pharm-micro:ceph.q: Aztreonam is safe in penicillin allergy because:
o: It is a carbapenem, not a penicillin
It is given orally, avoiding sensitization
It is a monobactam with no cross-reactivity
It lacks a β-lactam ring and cannot bind PBPs

pharm-micro:ceph.q: A 62-year-old man on mechanical ventilation in the ICU develops fever and purulent sputum. Sputum culture grows an oxidase-positive, lactose-nonfermenting gram-negative rod with a grape-like odor. Which cephalosporin would cover this organism?
pharm-micro:ceph.e: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is covered by the 4th-generation cefepime (and ceftazidime). Ceftriaxone lacks reliable antipseudomonal activity.

pharm-micro:vanco.q: Daptomycin should not be used for:
pharm-micro:vanco.e: Inactivated by pulmonary surfactant. Monitor CK for myopathy.

pharm-micro:vanco.q: A 66-year-old man on hemodialysis has fever; blood cultures grow catalase-negative gram-positive cocci that grow in 6.5% NaCl and hydrolyze bile esculin. The isolate is resistant to vancomycin. Mechanism of resistance?
o: Altered PBP2a with low β-lactam affinity
Efflux pump that exports the drug
pharm-micro:vanco.e: VRE (Enterococcus) replaces the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac, which vancomycin binds poorly. PBP2a (mecA) is the mechanism of MRSA.

pharm-micro:aminogly.q: Aminoglycosides are ineffective against anaerobes because:

A 68-year-old man receiving IV ampicillin plus gentamicin for enterococcal endocarditis develops tinnitus and an unsteady gait, and his creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL. The drug responsible for these effects acts by:
o: Inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Binding the 30S subunit, causing mRNA misreading
pharm-micro:aminogly.e: Gentamicin (aminoglycoside) causes ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; it binds the 30S subunit and blocks initiation/causes misreading. Ampicillin inhibits transpeptidation and lacks these toxicities.

pharm-micro:tetra.q: Tetracyclines should not be taken with:
pharm-micro:tetra.e: Divalent/trivalent cations chelate the drug → ↓ absorption.

pharm-micro:tetra.q: Tetracyclines are avoided in children because of:
o: Kernicterus from bilirubin displacement off albumin
Tooth discoloration and impaired bone growth
Gray baby syndrome and circulatory collapse

pharm-micro:tetra.q: A 30-year-old man from Connecticut has an expanding erythematous annular rash with central clearing on his thigh 10 days after a hiking trip, with fever and myalgia. The drug of choice acts by:
o: Blocking aminoacyl-tRNA binding at the 30S A site
pharm-micro:tetra.e: Early Lyme disease (erythema migrans) is treated with doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks tRNA attachment at the 30S A site. Macrolides block 50S translocation.

o: Red man syndrome with rapid infusion
Achilles tendon rupture in the elderly

pharm-micro:macro.e: Good anaerobic coverage above the diaphragm.

pharm-micro:macro.q: A 4-year-old unvaccinated girl has 2 weeks of paroxysmal coughing spells ending in an inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting. WBC is 32,000/mm³ with 75% lymphocytes. The drug of choice acts by:
pharm-micro:macro.e: Pertussis is treated with azithromycin, a macrolide that binds 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and blocks translocation. Tetracyclines act at the 30S A site.

pharm-micro:linezolid.q: A 58-year-old woman taking sertraline is started on an oral antibiotic for vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium bacteremia. Two days later she has agitation, hyperthermia, diaphoresis and inducible clonus. How does the new antibiotic kill bacteria?
o: Blocks aminoacyl-tRNA entry at the 30S site
Blocks formation of the 50S initiation complex
pharm-micro:linezolid.e: Linezolid (oral, VRE-active) is a weak MAO inhibitor that precipitates serotonin syndrome with SSRIs; it binds 23S rRNA and blocks the initiation complex. Daptomycin depolarizes membranes but is IV-only and not serotonergic.

o: Red man syndrome and tendon rupture
Tooth staining and gray baby syndrome
pharm-micro:folate.e: Also SJS, and kernicterus in neonates.

pharm-micro:folate.q: A 35-year-old man with HIV (CD4 120/mm³) takes TMP-SMX for Pneumocystis prophylaxis. Routine labs show K⁺ 6.1 mEq/L with normal renal function and no hemolysis. Mechanism of the hyperkalemia?
o: Trimethoprim blocks ENaC in the collecting duct
pharm-micro:folate.e: Trimethoprim acts like amiloride, blocking the collecting-duct epithelial Na⁺ channel and reducing K⁺ secretion. It does not inhibit aldosterone synthesis.

o: Red man syndrome on rapid infusion

pharm-micro:fq.q: A 72-year-old woman taking long-term prednisone for COPD is treated with levofloxacin for pneumonia. Five days later she feels a sudden pop in her posterior heel and cannot rise on her toes; squeezing the calf produces no plantar flexion. The antibiotic acts by:
o: Inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
pharm-micro:fq.e: Fluoroquinolones cause tendinopathy/Achilles rupture (higher risk with age and corticosteroids) and inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Rifampin inhibits RNA polymerase.

o: Red-orange body fluids and CYP induction
pharm-micro:tb.e: Give pyridoxine (B6). Ethambutol: optic neuritis; rifampin: orange fluids; pyrazinamide: hyperuricemia.

pharm-micro:tb.q: A 40-year-old man with cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis on four-drug therapy reports blurred vision; testing shows reduced acuity and red-green color blindness. The responsible drug acts by:
pharm-micro:tb.e: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis and blocks arabinosyltransferase (arabinogalactan synthesis). Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and causes peripheral neuropathy.

pharm-micro:prophylaxis.q: Pneumocystis prophylaxis in HIV begins at CD4 <:
Prophylaxis for MAC in HIV (when not on ART) at CD4 < 50:
pharm-micro:prophylaxis.e: Not needed if ART started promptly.

pharm-micro:prophylaxis.q: A 32-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. CD4 count is 80/mm³ and Toxoplasma IgG is positive. Which single drug provides the most appropriate primary prophylaxis?
pharm-micro:prophylaxis.e: TMP-SMX covers both Pneumocystis (CD4 < 200) and Toxoplasma (CD4 < 100, IgG+). Dapsone alone covers Pneumocystis but not Toxoplasma.

o: β-glucan synthase in the cell wall

pharm-micro:fungmap.e: Used for invasive Candida and Aspergillus.

pharm-micro:fungmap.q: A 65-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia and prolonged neutropenia develops fever and hemoptysis; CT shows a nodule with a surrounding halo. Biopsy shows septate hyphae branching at acute angles. The drug of choice acts by:
o: Binding ergosterol to form membrane pores
pharm-micro:fungmap.e: Invasive aspergillosis is treated with voriconazole, an azole that blocks ergosterol synthesis at 14α-demethylase. Amphotericin B binds ergosterol and is a second-line alternative.

pharm-micro:antiparasite.q: A 7-year-old girl has perianal itching that is worst at night. A cellophane tape test shows ova that are flattened on one side. She is treated with albendazole, which acts by:
pharm-micro:antiparasite.e: Enterobius vermicularis is treated with albendazole (or pyrantel); benzimidazoles bind β-tubulin. Increased Ca²⁺ permeability is praziquantel's mechanism.

o: Heme polymerase in the food vacuole

pharm-micro:malaria.q: Severe falciparum malaria is treated with:

A 28-year-old man returns from India with fevers recurring every 48 hours. Blood smear shows enlarged red cells with Schüffner dots. He is treated with chloroquine. Before adding a drug to prevent relapse, which test is required?
pharm-micro:malaria.e: P. vivax forms liver hypnozoites, eradicated by primaquine (or tafenoquine), which causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. HLA-B*57:01 is screened before abacavir.

pharm-micro:virmap.q: Acyclovir must be phosphorylated first by:

A 38-year-old man with AIDS (CD4 30/mm³) has blurred vision; fundoscopy shows fluffy yellow-white retinal lesions with hemorrhages. He is started on IV ganciclovir. Activation of this drug first requires:
o: No activation; binds the pyrophosphate site
pharm-micro:virmap.e: CMV retinitis: ganciclovir is monophosphorylated by the CMV UL97 kinase. Foscarnet needs no activation; HSV/VZV thymidine kinase activates acyclovir.

pharm-micro:hiv.q: A 34-year-old man is started on tenofovir, emtricitabine and efavirenz. Two weeks later he reports vivid dreams, insomnia and dizziness. The responsible drug acts by:
o: Blocking strand transfer by viral integrase
Competing with nucleotides at the RT active site
Binding reverse transcriptase at an allosteric site
Inhibiting cleavage of the gag-pol polyprotein
pharm-micro:hiv.e: Efavirenz (an NNRTI) causes CNS effects and binds RT away from the active site. Tenofovir and emtricitabine are NRTIs that compete at the active site.

pharm-micro:hep.q: A 40-year-old man has been HBsAg-positive for over 6 months. He is HBeAg-positive, HBV DNA is 2 × 10⁷ IU/mL and ALT is 3 times the upper limit of normal. He is started on tenofovir, which acts by:
o: Inhibiting the viral NS3/4A serine protease
Inhibiting the viral NS5B RNA polymerase
Blocking viral entry via the NTCP receptor
pharm-micro:hep.e: Chronic active hepatitis B is treated with tenofovir or entecavir, which inhibit the HBV polymerase's reverse transcriptase activity. NS5B and NS3/4A are hepatitis C targets.

micro-virol-1:vir-names.q: The reovirus was called an "orphan" virus because it was:
o: Unable to grow in any cultured cell line
Discovered before any disease was linked to it
Lacking a capsid recognisable on electron microscopy
Found during a survey of children in an orphanage
micro-virol-1:vir-names.e: Its name stands for respiratory, enteric, orphan.

micro-virol-1:vir-names.q: Which virus family is named after a structural feature rather than a disease or place?
micro-virol-1:vir-names.e: Toga is Greek for mantle and refers to the envelope surrounding the virion.

micro-virol-1:vir-names.q: A newly isolated virus is named for the town where the first outbreak occurred. Which existing virus follows the same convention?
micro-virol-1:vir-names.e: Norwalk, Ohio and Coxsackie, New York both gave their names to viruses, as did several African sites for togaviruses, arenaviruses and bunyaviruses.

micro-virol-1:vir-dna-fam.q: Which DNA virus family has a single-stranded linear genome?
micro-virol-1:vir-dna-fam.e: At 18 to 26 nm it is also the smallest of the DNA viruses.

micro-virol-1:vir-dna-fam.q: Which DNA virus carries its own polymerase inside the virion?
micro-virol-1:vir-dna-fam.e: It replicates in the cytoplasm, so it cannot borrow the nuclear enzymes of the cell.

micro-virol-1:vir-dna-fam.q: A brick-shaped enveloped virion measuring 300 by 240 by 100 nm is seen on electron microscopy. Which family is it, and why does its size matter clinically?
o: Adenoviridae, because of the fibres projecting from its capsid
Poxviridae, because it is almost visible by light microscopy
Herpesviridae, because its tegument makes the virion large
Hepadnaviridae, because its envelope adds to the diameter
micro-virol-1:vir-dna-fam.e: At about one-fourth the size of a staphylococcus, it is the largest virus of medical importance.

micro-virol-1:vir-rna-fam.q: Which statement about negative-strand RNA viruses is correct?
o: None of them carry a polymerase
All of them have segmented genomes
All of them are naked capsid viruses
micro-virol-1:vir-rna-fam.e: Their genome cannot be read as messenger RNA, so the polymerase must travel with it.

micro-virol-1:vir-rna-fam.q: An ambisense RNA genome means that the molecule:
o: Contains + and - regions joined end to end
Is read in both directions by the ribosome

micro-virol-1:vir-rna-fam.q: Why are there at least 13 RNA virus families but only seven DNA families?
o: RNA genomes take far more structural forms
RNA viruses are larger and so carry more genes
DNA viruses were discovered later than RNA viruses
RNA viruses lack capsids and so vary more in shape
micro-virol-1:vir-rna-fam.e: Positive sense, negative sense, double stranded, ambisense and segmented forms all exist, and families are defined by genome structure plus virion morphology.

micro-virol-1:vir-virion.q: The virion of a clinically important virus ranges in size from:
micro-virol-1:vir-virion.e: Parvovirus sets the lower limit and poxvirus the upper.

o: Capsid or nucleic acid-binding protein together with the genome
The viral envelope together with its glycoprotein spikes
The matrix protein layer lying under the viral envelope
The genome alone, stripped of all its associated protein
micro-virol-1:vir-virion.e: It may itself be the virion, or be surrounded by an envelope.

micro-virol-1:vir-virion.q: Antibody directed against the viral attachment protein prevents infection because:
o: It blocks the interaction with the target cell
It inhibits the polymerase carried in the virion
It digests the genome inside the intact virion
It lyses the cell that the virus has infected
micro-virol-1:vir-virion.e: Disrupting or removing the outer package inactivates the virus, and the attachment protein sits on that outer surface.

micro-virol-1:vir-capsid.q: The simple icosahedron of a picornavirus is built from:
micro-virol-1:vir-capsid.e: Each such capsomere is a pentamer, or penton.

micro-virol-1:vir-capsid.q: Capsomeres with six nearest neighbours are called:
micro-virol-1:vir-capsid.e: Inserting them between the pentons extends the icosahedron into an icosadeltahedron.

micro-virol-1:vir-capsid.q: The herpesvirus nucleocapsid has 12 pentons and 150 hexons. This tells you that the capsid is:
micro-virol-1:vir-capsid.e: The number of hexons inserted along the edges and surfaces sets the size of the extended icosahedron.

micro-virol-1:vir-naked-env.q: Which property follows directly from having no envelope?
o: Survival of passage through the gut
micro-virol-1:vir-naked-env.e: Naked capsids also resist acid, proteases, drying and poor sewage treatment.

o: Contaminated drinking water after sewage treatment
micro-virol-1:vir-naked-env.e: They are environmentally labile and must stay wet.

micro-virol-1:vir-naked-env.q: Why can an enveloped virus establish a persistent infection more readily than a naked capsid virus?
o: It can be released by budding without killing the cell
Its genome is always larger and more regulated
It replicates in the nucleus rather than cytoplasm
Its envelope makes it resistant to neutralising antibody
micro-virol-1:vir-naked-env.e: A naked capsid virus generally has to lyse the cell to get out.

micro-virol-1:vir-attach.q: The viral attachment protein of influenza A is the:
micro-virol-1:vir-attach.e: A viral attachment protein that also binds erythrocytes is called a hemagglutinin.

micro-virol-1:vir-attach.q: The viral attachment protein of adenovirus is the:
micro-virol-1:vir-attach.e: Rabies virus uses a G protein and reovirus uses sigma-1.

micro-virol-1:vir-attach.q: An arbovirus can infect mosquitoes, birds and mammals. The best explanation is that its attachment protein binds:
o: A protein found only in the gut of insects
Sialic acid and nothing else on any cell
Complement component C3b on the cell surface
A receptor expressed across many animal species
micro-virol-1:vir-attach.e: Receptor distribution is what sets host range and tissue tropism, and a widely distributed receptor allows an arthropod vector to carry the virus.

micro-virol-1:vir-enter.q: Influenza A fuses with the cell membrane:
o: In an endosome at acid pH
At the cell surface at neutral pH
Only after proteolytic cleavage by lysosomal enzymes
micro-virol-1:vir-enter.e: The mild acid of the endosome exposes the hydrophobic part of the hemagglutinin.

micro-virol-1:vir-enter.q: Which virus uses a fusion protein active at neutral pH and can also fuse cell to cell into syncytia?
micro-virol-1:vir-enter.e: Some herpesviruses and retroviruses also fuse at neutral pH and induce syncytia after replication.

micro-virol-1:vir-enter.q: Uncoating of the influenza nucleocapsid depends on the M2 protein because M2:
o: Transports the genome to the nucleus
Forms an ion pore that acidifies the virion
micro-virol-1:vir-enter.e: Protons flow from inside the endosome through that pore, which is why an M2 blocker stops replication at this step.

micro-virol-1:vir-synth.q: Which genome can function as messenger RNA immediately on entering the cell?
o: Positive-sense RNA of a non-retroviral virus
Double-stranded RNA held inside an intact core
Single-stranded DNA of a parvovirus genome
Negative-sense RNA with its polymerase attached
micro-virol-1:vir-synth.e: Naked DNA genomes other than poxvirus are also directly usable, by way of the nuclear machinery.

micro-virol-1:vir-synth.q: During the eclipse period of a growth curve:
o: Virus titre in the medium is maximal
No viral components can be seen
micro-virol-1:vir-synth.e: The latent period is the related interval during which no infectious virus is present in the medium.

micro-virol-1:vir-synth.q: A negative-strand RNA virus must package its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase because:
o: Its genome is too large for cellular enzymes
Its capsid cannot be uncoated otherwise
The cell has no enzyme that can read its genome
It replicates only in the nucleus
micro-virol-1:vir-synth.e: This is why the polymerase of orthomyxoviruses, paramyxoviruses and rhabdoviruses is bound to the genome inside the virion.

micro-virol-2:vp-steps.q: The prodrome of a viral illness is caused mainly by:
micro-virol-2:vp-steps.e: Fever, headache, body aches and chills are the usual form it takes.

micro-virol-2:vp-steps.q: A long incubation period suggests that the virus:
o: Does not induce interferon at the site of entry
Must spread and be amplified before reaching the target tissue
Is a naked capsid virus released only by cell lysis
Replicates unusually fast once it reaches the target
micro-virol-2:vp-steps.e: It is short when the primary site of infection is itself the target tissue.

micro-virol-2:vp-steps.q: Two patients are infected with the same dose of the same virus; one is asymptomatic and one is critically ill. Which factor is most likely to explain the difference?
o: The genetics of the particular viral strain
Immune status and competence of the host
The portal of entry used by the virus
The season of the year in which it was caught
micro-virol-2:vp-steps.e: Exposure route, dose, and viral and host genetics all matter, but once infection is established host immunity is the dominant determinant.

micro-virol-2:vp-entry.q: The most common route of viral infection is thought to be:
micro-virol-2:vp-entry.e: The respiratory tract offers a large mucoepithelial surface.

micro-virol-2:vp-entry.q: Which is NOT one of the defences protecting body orifices?
micro-virol-2:vp-entry.e: Keratinised skin protects the body surface, not the orifices.

micro-virol-2:vp-entry.q: After entry, a virus replicates only in cells that:
o: Express its receptor and have suitable biosynthetic machinery
Are phagocytic and take up the virion by endocytosis
Lack major histocompatibility complex I on the surface
Are actively dividing and so replicating their own DNA
micro-virol-2:vp-entry.e: This is why receptor distribution determines tissue tropism.

micro-virol-2:vp-spread.q: Picornaviruses and reoviruses reach the lymphatic system by binding receptors on:
o: Renal tubular cells of the nephron
micro-virol-2:vp-spread.e: The M cell translocates the virus to the lymphoid tissue beneath.

micro-virol-2:vp-spread.q: A secondary viremia typically follows replication in:
o: Macrophages, vascular endothelium, lung or liver
Peripheral nerves supplying the entry site
The epidermis at the original site of entry
The cerebrospinal fluid of the subarachnoid space
micro-virol-2:vp-spread.e: Replication at these sites amplifies the infection before the virus reaches the target tissue.

micro-virol-2:vp-spread.q: A virus is carried to the brain inside migrating macrophages rather than free in plasma. The practical consequence is that:
o: Interferon cannot be induced by the infection
Circulating antibody is less able to intercept it
The virus must be a naked capsid virus
It cannot cross the meninges into the brain
micro-virol-2:vp-spread.e: Cell-associated spread is one of the recognised ways viruses evade humoral immunity.

micro-virol-2:vp-celltypes.q: In a latent infection the cell:
micro-virol-2:vp-celltypes.e: A persistent productive infection, by contrast, yields virus and leads to senescence.

micro-virol-2:vp-celltypes.q: Transformation by a DNA virus differs from transformation by a retrovirus in that the DNA virus:
o: Cannot immortalise the cell that it transforms
Does not produce virus from the transformed cell
Requires a helper virus to transform the target cell
Always integrates its genome into a host chromosome
micro-virol-2:vp-celltypes.e: Retroviruses can produce virus and immortalise the cell at the same time.

micro-virol-2:vp-celltypes.q: An abortive infection is best described as one in which:
o: Virus is produced and the cell dies
Virus is produced and the cell survives
No virus is produced and the cell is unaffected
micro-virol-2:vp-celltypes.e: Nothing comes of the infection in either direction.

micro-virol-2:vp-cpe.q: Negri bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions seen in:
micro-virol-2:vp-cpe.e: Cowdry type A bodies are intranuclear and seen in herpes simplex virus infection.

micro-virol-2:vp-cpe.q: An "owl's eye" intranuclear basophilic inclusion in an enlarged cell suggests:
o: Measles virus in a giant cell
Rabies virus in a brain biopsy
micro-virol-2:vp-cpe.e: Adenovirus produces a similar intranuclear inclusion but without the cell enlargement.

micro-virol-2:vp-cpe.q: Syncytium formation is a cytopathic mechanism used by all of the following EXCEPT:
micro-virol-2:vp-cpe.e: Cell-to-cell fusion requires a fusion glycoprotein in a membrane, which a naked capsid virus does not have.

micro-virol-2:vp-onco.q: Approximately what fraction of human cancers is related to oncogenic viruses?
micro-virol-2:vp-onco.e: HTLV-1, hepatitis B and C, high-risk papillomaviruses, human herpesvirus 8 and Epstein-Barr virus are the recognised agents.

micro-virol-2:vp-onco.q: A DNA virus immortalises a cell only in a semipermissive cell because:
o: Only permissive cells express the receptor
Late proteins are needed for transformation
Full replication would kill the cell
micro-virol-2:vp-onco.e: Synthesis of viral DNA, late messenger RNA, late proteins or virus leads to cell death, which precludes immortalisation.

micro-virol-2:vp-onco.q: Immortalisation alone does not equal cancer. The best explanation is that immortalised cells:
o: Cannot divide beyond a fixed number of times
micro-virol-2:vp-onco.e: They are also more susceptible to cofactors and tumour promoters, so transformation is a step on the way rather than the destination.

micro-virol-2:vp-defense.q: The innate antiviral response differs from the innate response to bacteria mainly in that it:
o: Is mediated largely by interferon and cytokines
Begins only after several days have passed
Depends on complement and neutrophil recruitment
Requires prior exposure to the same organism
micro-virol-2:vp-defense.e: That is why the first symptoms are flulike rather than inflammatory.

micro-virol-2:vp-defense.q: Which arm of immunity is essential to prevent viremic spread to the target tissue?
micro-virol-2:vp-defense.e: Cell-mediated responses are better at limiting local spread.

micro-virol-2:vp-defense.q: Hepatitis A virus is non-cytolytic. Which host response is therefore required to clear infected cells?
micro-virol-2:vp-defense.e: Antibody can control a cytolytic virus because replication destroys the factory anyway, but a cell that is not killed by the virus must be killed by the host.

micro-virol-2:vp-escape.q: Cytomegalovirus and adenovirus evade T-cell killing by:
o: Blocking activation of the complement cascade
Changing their surface antigens from year to year
Forming syncytia so they never leave the cell
Inhibiting major histocompatibility complex I expression
micro-virol-2:vp-escape.e: Without surface presentation the infected cell is invisible to cytotoxic T cells.

micro-virol-2:vp-escape.q: Antigenic shift and drift in influenza limit the efficacy of:
micro-virol-2:vp-escape.e: Human immunodeficiency virus achieves the same thing by varying within a single infected person.

micro-virol-2:vp-escape.q: Herpes simplex virus continues to synthesise protein despite interferon because it:
o: Replicates only in neurons, where interferon is low
Blocks the antiviral state induced by IFN-alpha and IFN-beta
Does not induce any interferon in the first place
Lacks the double-stranded RNA intermediates that trigger it
micro-virol-2:vp-escape.e: Preventing the consequences of the antiviral state is a distinct escape strategy from preventing interferon production.

micro-virol-2:vp-immunopath.q: The classic symptoms of measles, mumps and the hepatitis viruses are produced mainly by:
micro-virol-2:vp-immunopath.e: Enveloped viruses in general induce cell-mediated responses with wide immunopathology.

micro-virol-2:vp-immunopath.q: Immune complexes formed during chronic hepatitis B infection most characteristically deposit in the:
micro-virol-2:vp-immunopath.e: Complement activation by those complexes drives the inflammation and tissue destruction.

micro-virol-2:vp-immunopath.q: A child with previous dengue infection develops dengue hemorrhagic fever on a second, different serotype. Which mechanism contributes?
o: Major histocompatibility complex expression is lost on infected cells
Interferon production fails entirely during the second illness
Non-neutralising antibody carries virus into macrophages via Fc receptors
Memory T cells are completely absent at the second exposure
micro-virol-2:vp-immunopath.e: Enhanced antigen-specific T-cell and antibody responses also damage infected endothelial cells, which is why partial immunity makes the second illness worse.

micro-virol-2:vp-determinants.q: Tissue tropism of a virus is determined chiefly by:
o: Whether the virus is enveloped or a naked capsid virus
The length of the incubation period before symptoms
Specificity of the viral attachment protein and receptor distribution
The size of the viral genome and the number of its genes
micro-virol-2:vp-determinants.e: The cell must also be permissive for replication.

micro-virol-2:vp-determinants.q: Which property allows an enteric virus to reach the bloodstream from the gut?
micro-virol-2:vp-determinants.e: An enveloped virus could not survive that passage.

micro-virol-2:vp-determinants.q: An inapparent infection can still matter to public health because:
o: The person can still transmit the virus
It is more likely to be oncogenic
It always progresses to chronic disease
micro-virol-2:vp-determinants.e: Absence of symptoms reflects the tissue infected and the host response, not absence of virus.

micro-virol-3:vl-specimen.q: Specimens for viral isolation should be collected:
o: During convalescence, once antibody has risen
Only once the symptoms have fully resolved
After antibody has appeared in the serum
Early in the acute phase, before shedding stops
micro-virol-3:vl-specimen.e: Respiratory viruses may be shed for only 3 to 7 days, sometimes stopping before symptoms do.

micro-virol-3:vl-specimen.q: Enveloped viruses such as herpes simplex and influenza lose infectious titre when:
o: Held at room temperature or frozen at minus 20 degrees
Delivered to the laboratory within a few hours
Placed in a medium containing serum albumin
Transported to the laboratory on wet ice
micro-virol-3:vl-specimen.e: Non-enveloped viruses such as adenovirus and enterovirus are far less affected.

micro-virol-3:vl-specimen.q: A patient develops focal encephalitis localised to the temporal lobe after several days of headache and disorientation. Which specimen and test should be prioritised?
o: Serum for arbovirus serology and nothing else
Cerebrospinal fluid for herpes simplex virus PCR
Nasal washing for a respiratory virus panel
Stool for enterovirus culture and typing
micro-virol-3:vl-specimen.e: The clinical picture points to one virus, and its DNA can be detected in that fluid relatively quickly.

micro-virol-3:vl-cyto.q: A multinucleated giant cell formed by virus-induced cell fusion is called a:
micro-virol-3:vl-cyto.e: Paramyxoviruses, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus and human immunodeficiency virus all produce them.

micro-virol-3:vl-cyto.q: Hemadsorption in a cell culture indicates that the infected cells are expressing:
micro-virol-3:vl-cyto.e: Influenza, mumps, parainfluenza and togaviruses can be detected this way.

micro-virol-3:vl-cyto.q: Immunoelectron microscopy improves detection of enteric viruses because adding specific antibody:
o: Clumps the particles and identifies them at the same time
Removes bacterial debris from the stool sample
Stains the viral genome inside the capsid
Increases the number of particles in the specimen
micro-virol-3:vl-cyto.e: Rotavirus is abundant in stool and has a characteristic morphology, which makes it a good target for the method.

micro-virol-3:vl-culture.q: The TCD50 of a virus is the titre that:
o: Causes cytopathologic effects in half the cultured cells
Gives a fourfold rise in antibody titre
Produces exactly one plaque per culture well
Kills half of a set of inoculated test animals
micro-virol-3:vl-culture.e: LD50 and ID50 are the equivalent measures in animals.

micro-virol-3:vl-culture.q: Which is NOT a system used to propagate viruses?
micro-virol-3:vl-culture.e: Viruses require living cells, so a bacteriological agar plate is of no use.

micro-virol-3:vl-culture.q: The ratio of viral particles counted by electron microscopy to plaque-forming units is always much greater than one because:
o: Cell cultures are only partly permissive
micro-virol-3:vl-culture.e: Defective particles are generated routinely during replication, so they are visible but not infectious.

micro-virol-3:vl-genome.q: Real-time PCR is particularly valuable because it:
o: Needs no primers and so no sequence data
Works only on genomes made of DNA
Quantifies the genome and therefore the virus load
Detects antibody as well as viral genome
micro-virol-3:vl-genome.e: The concentration of genome is proportional to the initial rate of amplification.

micro-virol-3:vl-genome.q: RT-PCR differs from conventional PCR in that it first:
o: Amplifies the genome a millionfold in one step
Hybridises a luminescent probe to the target
Converts viral RNA to DNA using reverse transcriptase
micro-virol-3:vl-genome.e: Only then can the sequence be amplified.

micro-virol-3:vl-genome.q: In situ hybridisation is especially useful for cytomegalovirus and human papillomavirus because these viruses:
o: Lack genomes detectable by any probe
Are too dangerous to grow in culture
micro-virol-3:vl-genome.e: The probe detects the virus even without replication, which is also why it helps when viral antigen cannot be found immunologically.

micro-virol-3:vl-sero.q: Detection of virus-specific IgM generally indicates:
micro-virol-3:vl-sero.e: It is present during the first two or three weeks of a primary infection.

micro-virol-3:vl-sero.q: Seroconversion is defined as an antibody titre rise of at least:
o: Fourfold between acute and convalescent sera
Any rise that the laboratory can detect
Twofold within the first 24 hours of illness
Tenfold at any point during the illness
micro-virol-3:vl-sero.e: The convalescent sample is taken at least two to three weeks after the acute one.

micro-virol-3:vl-sero.q: Serology for parainfluenza is positive in a patient who actually has mumps. The most likely explanation is:
o: Use of an overly specific monoclonal antibody
micro-virol-3:vl-sero.e: The opposite problem, an antibody too specific to recognise related strains, produces false negatives instead, as happens with rhinovirus.

micro-virol-3:va-targets.q: Oseltamivir and zanamivir act at which step of influenza replication?
o: Uncoating, by blocking the M2 channel
micro-virol-3:va-targets.e: Amantadine and rimantadine act at the penetration and uncoating step instead.

micro-virol-3:va-targets.q: Interferon is approved for clinical use against:
micro-virol-3:va-targets.e: It blocks transcription and protein synthesis in the infected cell.

micro-virol-3:va-targets.q: Ribavirin promotes hypermutation of the viral genome. The effect is best compared to:
o: Reading a whole sentence from back to front
Replacing every fourth letter of an essay at random
Photocopying a single page of a book twice
Deleting the last page of a long book
micro-virol-3:va-targets.e: Enough random substitutions make the gene products non-functional, which is a different mechanism from chain termination.

micro-virol-3:va-nucleoside.q: Nucleoside analogs are selective for viral polymerases because those enzymes:
o: Lack a proofreading domain only in RNA viruses
Are less accurate and bind the analogs far better
micro-virol-3:va-nucleoside.e: The viral enzyme binds modified nucleosides several hundred times better than the host enzyme.

micro-virol-3:va-nucleoside.q: Acyclovir receives its first phosphate from:
micro-virol-3:va-nucleoside.e: Cellular enzymes add the remaining two phosphates.

micro-virol-3:va-nucleoside.q: A patient with recurrent herpes simplex infection no longer responds to acyclovir. The most likely mechanism is:
o: Loss of viral thymidine kinase activity
A mutation in the host polymerase
micro-virol-3:va-nucleoside.e: Without the viral enzyme the drug is never activated, so the step that gave it selectivity is also the step that resistance targets.

micro-virol-3:va-control.q: Compared with enveloped viruses, naked capsid viruses are:
micro-virol-3:va-control.e: Most enveloped viruses are inactivated by soap and detergents alone.

micro-virol-3:va-control.q: Universal precautions require that all human blood be treated as if contaminated with:
o: No virus unless the patient is known positive
Human immunodeficiency virus or hepatitis B virus
micro-virol-3:va-control.e: Special care is also needed with needles and contaminated surgical tools.

micro-virol-3:va-control.q: The first step in controlling an outbreak of hepatitis A is to:
o: Quarantine every contact of every case
Vaccinate the whole of the affected community
Begin antiviral therapy for all cases
Identify the food, water or facility that is the source
micro-virol-3:va-control.e: Identifying the source or reservoir precedes cleanup, quarantine and immunisation.

micro-virol-4:hpv-struct.q: The viral attachment protein of human papillomavirus is:
micro-virol-4:hpv-struct.e: Antibody against it neutralises the virus, which is the basis of the vaccine.

micro-virol-4:hpv-struct.q: Late genes of human papillomavirus are expressed only in the:
o: Basal cell layer, where the virus first enters
Stratum spinosum, midway through the epidermis
Dermis, beneath the epithelial basement membrane
micro-virol-4:hpv-struct.e: The virus assembles in the nucleus there and is shed with the dead surface cells.

micro-virol-4:hpv-struct.q: Why is the replication cycle of human papillomavirus tied to keratinocyte differentiation?
o: The viral DNA polymerase works only at the epithelial surface
Different layers express different nuclear factors that switch viral genes on
The virus can only enter cells that are fully differentiated
Only the superficial cells of the epithelium carry the receptor
micro-virol-4:hpv-struct.e: Viral gene expression tracks keratin expression, so the programme of the cell dictates the programme of the virus.

o: An epithelial cell containing a basophilic owl's eye inclusion
A multinucleated giant cell formed by fusion of keratinocytes
A basal cell showing abundant abnormal mitotic figures
An enlarged keratinocyte with a clear halo around a shrunken nucleus
micro-virol-4:hpv-dis.e: It is characteristic of papillomavirus infection.

micro-virol-4:hpv-dis.q: Which two human papillomavirus types account for about 70% of cervical carcinomas?
micro-virol-4:hpv-dis.e: Types 6 and 11 cause laryngeal papillomas acquired through an infected birth canal.

micro-virol-4:hpv-dis.q: Integration of the human papillomavirus genome promotes carcinogenesis because the break occurs in E1 or E2, which:
o: Removes the origin of replication and nothing else
Inactivates them and leaves E6 and E7 unregulated
Prevents the virus from entering the host cell
Destroys the genes encoding the capsid proteins
micro-virol-4:hpv-dis.e: The virus can no longer replicate, but the oncogenes keep being expressed.

micro-virol-4:polyoma.q: The polyomavirus T antigen promotes cell growth by binding:
micro-virol-4:polyoma.e: High-risk papillomaviruses split the same job between E6 and E7.

micro-virol-4:polyoma.q: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by:
micro-virol-4:polyoma.e: BK virus is associated with renal disease in the immunosuppressed.

micro-virol-4:polyoma.q: In progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy the demyelination occurs because the virus:
micro-virol-4:polyoma.e: It partially transforms astrocytes at the same time, which is why the lesions contain unusually large astrocytes.

micro-virol-4:adeno.q: Which part of the adenovirus virion carries the viral attachment protein?
micro-virol-4:adeno.e: The penton base and fiber are also toxic to cells.

micro-virol-4:adeno.q: The receptor used by most adenoviruses is shared with:
o: Influenza A, which uses sialic acid
micro-virol-4:adeno.e: Hence its name, the coxsackie adenovirus receptor.

micro-virol-4:adeno.q: Study of the adenovirus hexon gene led directly to the discovery of:
o: The triplet nature of the genetic code
micro-virol-4:adeno.e: That is one reason this virus has been used so heavily as a model system, and now as a gene-therapy vector.

micro-virol-4:parvo.e: Its tiny genome depends on a growing cell to supply the machinery.

micro-virol-4:parvo.q: The rash and arthralgia of erythema infectiosum coincide with:
o: Reticulocytopenia in the peripheral blood film
Peak viremia in the first days of the illness
Appearance of specific antibody and immune complexes
The prodrome, before any rash has appeared
micro-virol-4:parvo.e: The second stage of the illness is immune mediated, not directly cytopathic.

micro-virol-4:parvo.q: A child with sickle cell anaemia becomes severely anaemic after a viral illness. The mechanism combining with B19 infection is:
o: Autoimmune haemolysis of circulating mature red cells
Iron deficiency arising from chronic occult blood loss
A shortened erythrocyte lifespan from the underlying anaemia
Fibrosis of the marrow cavity caused by the virus
micro-virol-4:parvo.e: Depletion of red cell precursors is tolerated in a normal host but not when the cells already turn over fast.

micro-virol-4:pox.q: Poxviruses can replicate entirely in the cytoplasm because they encode:
o: An integrase that works on host DNA
A reverse transcriptase carried in the virion
A nuclear localisation signal on the capsid
Their own DNA-dependent RNA and DNA polymerases
micro-virol-4:pox.e: Every other DNA virus of medical importance must reach the nucleus.

micro-virol-4:pox.q: Which feature distinguishes the rash of smallpox?
o: All vesicles appear at the same time
The rash spares the palms and soles
micro-virol-4:pox.e: Varicella, by contrast, produces lesions of different ages together.

micro-virol-4:pox.q: Uncoating of poxvirus happens in two stages because:
o: The genome is circular and has to be linearised beforehand
Virion enzymes must first make messenger RNA for an uncoating enzyme
The envelope is far too thick to be removed in a single step
The capsid is helical and can only unwind gradually
micro-virol-4:pox.e: The partially uncoated subviral particle makes the enzyme that then releases the DNA core.

micro-virol-5:hv-family.q: Which herpesvirus becomes latent in memory B cells?
micro-virol-5:hv-family.e: Cytomegalovirus hides in haematopoietic progenitors and monocytes instead.

micro-virol-5:hv-family.q: The space between the herpesvirus capsid and its envelope is the:
micro-virol-5:hv-family.e: It carries proteins and enzymes that help start replication once the virion is inside.

micro-virol-5:hv-family.q: Herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus and varicella-zoster virus can form isomeric genomes because:
o: Recombination between inverted repeats flips the unique segments
They have segmented genomes that reassort on co-infection
Their genomes are circular rather than linear molecules
They integrate into a chromosome of the infected host
micro-virol-5:hv-family.e: Direct and inverted repeats bracket the unique long and unique short regions, allowing both circularisation and internal recombination.

micro-virol-5:hv-repl.q: In which phase of herpesvirus transcription is the viral DNA polymerase made?
micro-virol-5:hv-repl.e: Immediate early proteins regulate transcription; late proteins are mainly structural.

micro-virol-5:hv-repl.q: Herpesviruses can replicate in neurons, which lack deoxyribonucleotides, because the virus encodes:
o: A reverse transcriptase to copy the genome
An integrase that inserts the viral genome
Scavenging enzymes that supply nucleotide substrates
A cellular RNA polymerase of its own
micro-virol-5:hv-repl.e: Those same enzymes make the virus able to replicate in non-growing cells.

micro-virol-5:hv-repl.q: A cell transcribes a special limited set of viral genes without replicating the genome. This produces:
o: An abortive infection with cell death
micro-virol-5:hv-repl.e: Progression to early and late gene expression instead yields virus production and usually kills the cell.

micro-virol-5:hsv-latency.q: During latency in a neuron, the only region of the herpes simplex virus genome transcribed produces:
micro-virol-5:hsv-latency.e: Those RNAs are not translated but encode micro-RNAs that silence immediate early genes.

micro-virol-5:hsv-latency.q: Which host factors are important for maintaining herpes simplex virus latency?
o: CD8 T cells and interferon gamma
micro-virol-5:hsv-latency.e: Latency is actively maintained, not simply a dormant state.

micro-virol-5:hsv-latency.q: A patient develops a cold sore in the same spot after every episode of sunburn. The best explanation is that reactivation:
o: Circulating antibody has to be lost before a recurrence can occur
The lip is reinfected from virus shed continuously in the saliva
A different strain of the virus is acquired on each exposure
Occurs in one neuron of the ganglion and travels back down the same nerve
micro-virol-5:hsv-latency.e: The virus reactivates despite circulating antibody, which is why recurrences happen at all.

micro-virol-5:hsv-dis.q: The classic herpes simplex lesion is described as:
o: A clear vesicle on an erythematous base
A pustule with a necrotic centre
micro-virol-5:hsv-dis.e: It then progresses to pustules, ulcers and crusted lesions.

micro-virol-5:hsv-dis.q: Herpetic whitlow is an infection of the:
micro-virol-5:hsv-dis.e: Herpes gladiatorum, affecting the body, is often acquired during wrestling or rugby.

micro-virol-5:hsv-dis.q: A child with active eczema develops widespread herpes simplex lesions. This happens because:
o: Eczema suppresses systemic immunity to the virus
The virus mutates as it replicates in damaged skin
The skin disease lets infection spread along the skin
Antibody cannot be formed while eczema is active
micro-virol-5:hsv-dis.e: Eczema herpeticum may spread to the adrenal glands, liver and other organs.

micro-virol-5:vzv.q: How does the rash of varicella differ from that of zoster?
o: Varicella lesions are present in all stages at once
Varicella follows a single dermatome of the trunk
Zoster spares the trunk and affects only the face
Zoster lesions all appear at the very same time
micro-virol-5:vzv.e: Zoster appears along the whole length of one dermatome.

micro-virol-5:vzv.q: Postherpetic neuralgia develops in approximately what proportion of zoster patients?
micro-virol-5:vzv.e: It can persist for months to years.

micro-virol-5:vzv.q: Higher doses of acyclovir are needed for varicella-zoster virus than for herpes simplex virus because:
o: It does not encode a thymidine kinase at all
It replicates in the cytoplasm, away from the drug
Its DNA polymerase is much less sensitive to the drug
It is a naked capsid virus and excludes the drug
micro-virol-5:vzv.e: Famciclovir and valaciclovir are alternatives with better pharmacodynamics.

micro-virol-5:ebv.q: The atypical lymphocytes of infectious mononucleosis are:
micro-virol-5:ebv.e: They are also called Downey cells, and may make up 10% to 80% of the white cell count in the second week.

micro-virol-5:ebv.q: The heterophile antibody of infectious mononucleosis is an IgM directed against:
micro-virol-5:ebv.e: It recognises that antigen on sheep, horse or bovine erythrocytes.

micro-virol-5:ebv.q: A boy with a congenital T-cell defect acquires Epstein-Barr virus and develops a polyclonal leukaemia-like B-cell proliferation rather than mononucleosis. The reason is that:
o: The virus mutates in T-cell deficiency
B cells cannot present antigen in this condition
T cells normally control the proliferating B cells
micro-virol-5:ebv.e: Mononucleosis is essentially the T-cell response itself, so without T cells the B-cell outgrowth is unchecked.

o: The agent responsible for Kaposi sarcoma
The most common viral cause of congenital defects
A virus that becomes latent in sensory neurons
A cause of roseola in infants and young children
micro-virol-5:cmv.e: About 1 in 150 children is born infected.

micro-virol-5:cmv.q: Which human herpesvirus causes Kaposi sarcoma?
micro-virol-5:cmv.e: HHV-6 and HHV-7 cause roseola instead.

micro-virol-5:cmv.q: Antiviral drugs active against herpes simplex and varicella-zoster virus depend on an enzyme encoded by those viruses, namely:
micro-virol-5:cmv.e: It applies the first phosphate to the nucleoside analog, which is why loss of that enzyme confers resistance.

micro-virol-6:picorna-struct.q: Naked picornavirus RNA injected into a cell is infectious on its own because the genome:
o: Integrates into the host chromosome first
Is double-stranded and so needs no copying
Carries its own RNA polymerase in the virion
Is plus-sense and acts directly as messenger RNA
micro-virol-6:picorna-struct.e: VPg and the 3' polyA tail raise its infectivity, but what makes it sufficient is that ribosomes can translate it immediately.

micro-virol-6:picorna-struct.q: Pleconaril blocks picornavirus uncoating by binding:
o: The internal ribosome entry site of the genome
The canyon floor in VP1 where the receptor docks
micro-virol-6:picorna-struct.e: Its 3-methylisoxazole group distorts the canyon so the capsid cannot be destabilised.

micro-virol-6:picorna-struct.q: Which capsid polypeptide is cleaved from VP0 only after the genome has been packaged, and is released when the virus binds its receptor?
micro-virol-6:picorna-struct.e: VP0 is cleaved into VP2 and VP4; VP4 stabilises the mature virion and leaves on receptor binding.

micro-virol-6:picorna-struct.q: A picornavirus messenger RNA has no 5' cap. Ribosomes still load onto it by recognising:
o: A cellular cap donated by the host
micro-virol-6:picorna-struct.e: The same loop structure is found in a few cellular messenger RNAs.
Receptor specificity, not the genome, is the main determinant of which tissue each picornavirus damages.

micro-virol-6:entero.q: A child develops acute flaccid paralysis of one leg after a febrile illness. The virus has destroyed:
o: Motor neurons of the anterior horn
Dorsal root ganglia of the spinal cord
The neuromuscular junction of the limb
micro-virol-6:entero.e: Poliovirus infection of anterior horn and brainstem motor neurons is cytolytic, hence flaccid rather than spastic weakness.

micro-virol-6:entero.q: Herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease are caused by:
micro-virol-6:entero.e: Group B is remembered for body disease — pleurodynia, myocarditis — while group A gives the vesicular lesions.

micro-virol-6:entero.q: Enteroviruses survive passage through the stomach and mild sewage treatment because the capsid:
o: Is stable from pH 3 to 9 and resists detergent
Is enveloped and resists bile salts
micro-virol-6:entero.e: Rhinovirus is the exception within the family: it is acid-labile.

o: Replicate in the gut but do not cause enteric disease
Cause watery diarrhoea as their main illness
micro-virol-6:entero.e: First-round replication may be in oropharynx, respiratory tract or gastrointestinal tract, but disease comes from the lytic infection of a target tissue elsewhere.

o: It causes a characteristically biphasic illness
It was first isolated from the middle ear
The virus was found before any disease was attributed to it
It echoes the clinical picture of poliovirus disease
micro-virol-6:entero.e: Enteric cytopathic human orphan — an orphan virus is one without a known disease.

micro-virol-6:rhino.q: Rhinovirus infection stays in the upper respiratory tract because the virus:
o: Cannot cross the epithelial basement membrane
Is cleared rapidly by alveolar macrophages
Is acid-labile and replicates poorly above 33 °C
Binds only to mucin in the nasal cavity
micro-virol-6:rhino.e: Both properties together confine it; the nose is cooler than the core.

micro-virol-6:rhino.q: At least 80% of rhinovirus serotypes attach to:
micro-virol-6:rhino.e: That receptor is present on epithelial cells, fibroblasts and endothelial cells.

micro-virol-6:rhino.q: Why do enteroviruses spread by the faecal-oral route while rhinoviruses do not?
o: Rhinovirus is inactivated by gastric acid
micro-virol-6:rhino.e: Acid stability is the single difference that sends the two groups to different body sites.

micro-virol-6:corona.q: Coronaviruses resist detergent despite having an envelope because:
o: The envelope is cross-linked by matrix protein
A dense glycoprotein corona covers the envelope
The genome is protected by VPg
micro-virol-6:corona.e: This is the standing exception to the rule that enveloped viruses are detergent-sensitive.

micro-virol-6:corona.q: SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV cause systemic disease and severe pneumonia, unlike other human coronaviruses, because they:
micro-virol-6:corona.e: Most human coronaviruses have an optimum of 33 to 35 °C and so stay in the upper airway.

micro-virol-6:corona.q: The coronavirus protein that mediates both attachment and membrane fusion, and is the target of neutralising antibody, is:
micro-virol-6:corona.e: E1 is the transmembrane matrix protein; E3 hemagglutinin neuraminidase is present only in some strains.

micro-virol-6:corona.q: Coronaviruses account for roughly what share of all upper respiratory tract infections?
micro-virol-6:corona.e: Their cold is like a rhinovirus cold but with a longer incubation period, averaging 3 days.

micro-virol-6:noro.q: Norovirus outbreaks are hard to contain on cruise ships mainly because the virus:
o: Is highly resistant to the environment and to disinfectants
Is spread by a mosquito vector on board
Causes a prolonged viraemia with no symptoms at all
Has an animal reservoir on the ship
micro-virol-6:noro.e: It is a small capsid virus with a plus-sense RNA genome, resistant even to detergent.

micro-virol-6:noro.q: Norovirus produces watery diarrhoea with nausea and vomiting by:
micro-virol-6:noro.e: Treatment is supportive; diagnosis rests on symptoms plus RT-PCR of the genome.

micro-virol-6:paramyxo.q: The paramyxovirus fusion protein can only fuse membranes after:
o: Binding sialic acid on the cell surface
Proteolytic cleavage into F1 and F2 held by a disulfide bond
Phosphorylation by the L protein of the nucleocapsid
Removal of the matrix protein layer
micro-virol-6:paramyxo.e: Availability of the activating protease therefore helps decide which tissues the virus can infect.

micro-virol-6:paramyxo.q: Which paramyxovirus attachment protein carries neuraminidase activity?
o: HN of parainfluenza and mumps virus
micro-virol-6:paramyxo.e: HN binds sialic acid, so the virus must cleave sialic acid to avoid self-aggregation and to leave the cell; measles and respiratory syncytial virus bind protein receptors and need none.

micro-virol-6:paramyxo.q: The multinucleated giant cell formed in paramyxovirus infection is called a:
micro-virol-6:paramyxo.e: Respiratory syncytial virus is named for exactly this effect.

micro-virol-6:paramyxo.q: Which protein of the paramyxovirus nucleocapsid is the RNA polymerase?
micro-virol-6:paramyxo.e: P assists RNA synthesis and N maintains genome structure; the polymerase enters the cell as part of the nucleocapsid.

micro-virol-6:paramyxo.q: Paramyxovirus progeny leave the cell by:
o: Lysing the cell they have infected
Budding from the plasma membrane without killing it
micro-virol-6:paramyxo.e: Much of the tissue damage therefore comes from the cell-mediated immune response rather than from the virus itself.

micro-virol-6:measles.q: Small grey lesions in the mouth before the maculopapular rash of measles are:
micro-virol-6:measles.e: They accompany high fever, cough, conjunctivitis, coryza and photophobia.

micro-virol-6:measles.q: Measles virus spreads throughout the body as a viraemia in dendritic cells and lymphocytes because it binds:
micro-virol-6:measles.e: CD46 and nectin-4 give it access to epithelial and other cells; CD150 gives it the lymphoid route.

micro-virol-6:measles.q: A neurological complication of measles appearing 5 to 7 years after the illness is:
o: Postmeasles encephalitis in the acute phase
micro-virol-6:measles.e: It is caused by a measles variant; postmeasles encephalitis follows the acute illness instead.

micro-virol-6:measles.q: A child with a T-cell deficiency who catches measles is at particular risk of:
micro-virol-6:measles.e: Measles is also more severe where vitamin A is deficient.

micro-virol-6:measles.q: Measles remains a major cause of death worldwide — about how many deaths in 2012?
micro-virol-6:measles.e: There were more than 10 million cases a year in unvaccinated populations; a live attenuated vaccine prevents it.

micro-virol-6:mumps-rsv.q: A barking, seal-like cough in a toddler suggests croup caused by:
micro-virol-6:mumps-rsv.e: Parainfluenza also causes common cold, bronchitis and pneumonia.

micro-virol-6:mumps-rsv.q: Parotitis with orchitis and aseptic meningitis in an unvaccinated adolescent points to:
micro-virol-6:mumps-rsv.e: A live attenuated vaccine prevents it, as it does measles.

micro-virol-6:mumps-rsv.q: Which virus is a life-threatening cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in premature infants, prevented by passive immunisation in high-risk babies?
micro-virol-6:mumps-rsv.e: Aerosol ribavirin is the antiviral option.

micro-virol-6:flu-struct.q: Influenza A and B differ from every other RNA virus of the respiratory tract in that they:
o: Transcribe and replicate the genome in the nucleus
Assemble their virions in the Golgi
Lack a polymerase of their own
Have a plus-sense genome acting as messenger RNA
micro-virol-6:flu-struct.e: Assembly and budding still happen at the plasma membrane.

micro-virol-6:flu-struct.q: Amantadine is useless against influenza B because its target, the M2 ion channel:
o: Is encoded only by influenza A
micro-virol-6:flu-struct.e: Zanamivir, oseltamivir and peramivir inhibit the neuraminidase of both A and B.

micro-virol-6:flu-struct.q: Baloxavir marboxil works by blocking the step in which influenza polymerase:
o: Adds a polyA tail to each transcript
Snatches caps from cellular messenger RNA to prime its own
Exports the new nucleocapsids out of the nucleus
Cleaves hemagglutinin into its active form
micro-virol-6:flu-struct.e: The polymerase complex is PB1, PB2 and PA, bound with nucleoprotein to each negative-sense segment.

micro-virol-6:flu-struct.q: How many genome segments does influenza A carry?
micro-virol-6:flu-struct.e: Influenza C has seven; each segment is 890 to 2340 bases, and NS1 with NS2 and M1 with M2 share a segment each.

micro-virol-6:flu-struct.q: The extensive destruction of ciliated epithelium in influenza explains why patients:
micro-virol-6:flu-struct.e: The acute flu-like symptoms themselves come from massive cytokine release.

micro-virol-6:flu-drift.q: A new influenza pandemic strain arises when:
o: Genome segments reassort between a human and an animal virus in a co-infected host
Point mutations accumulate in the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes
Neuraminidase is lost from the virion surface
The virus integrates into the host chromosome
micro-virol-6:flu-drift.e: Accumulated mutation — antigenic drift — gives the annual epidemics instead.

micro-virol-6:flu-drift.q: Antigenic drift is possible because the influenza polymerase:
micro-virol-6:flu-drift.e: The segmented genome then adds reassortment on top of mutation.

micro-virol-6:flu-drift.q: Influenza A, unlike influenza B, is:
o: A zoonosis infecting humans, other mammals and birds
Restricted to children under five years
Unable to cause pneumonia in healthy adults
Without any neuraminidase on its surface
micro-virol-6:flu-drift.e: Only influenza A therefore has an animal reservoir in which reassortment can generate pandemic strains.

micro-virol-6:flu-drift.q: The live attenuated influenza vaccine given by nasal spray is licensed for people aged:
micro-virol-6:flu-drift.e: The inactivated vaccine contains hemagglutinin and neuraminidase of two influenza A strains and one or two influenza B strains.

micro-virol-7:rabies-struct.q: The characteristic bullet shape of the rabies virion is produced when the nucleocapsid associates with the:
micro-virol-7:rabies-struct.e: M lies between envelope and nucleocapsid, and binding to it makes the nucleocapsid coil into its condensed form.

micro-virol-7:rabies-struct.q: Rabies virus buds efficiently from the plasma membrane in only one tissue, which is why that tissue spreads the disease:
micro-virol-7:rabies-struct.e: In most cells the virus buds from intracytoplasmic membranes and release is inefficient.

micro-virol-7:rabies-struct.q: Transcription of the rabies genome into its five messenger RNAs takes place in:
micro-virol-7:rabies-struct.e: The polymerase is the L and NS proteins, carried into the cell as part of the nucleocapsid.

micro-virol-7:rabies-struct.q: Which rabies protein generates neutralising antibody?
micro-virol-7:rabies-struct.e: It covers the surface as a trimeric spike and is the viral attachment protein; that of vesicular stomatitis virus was the prototype for studying eukaryotic glycoprotein processing.

micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.q: Rabies virus reaches the spinal cord from a bite wound by:
micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.e: It first replicates quietly in muscle at the site of the bite for days to months.

micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.q: The length of the rabies incubation period is determined mainly by:
o: Infectious dose and proximity of the wound to the brain
Whether the biting animal was wild or domestic
The ambient temperature at the time
The blood group of the bitten patient
micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.e: Severity of the wound and the host's age and immune status also contribute.

micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.q: Post-exposure vaccination can still prevent rabies because:
o: Rabies virus is cleared by cell-mediated immunity once primed
The virus is unable to cross the blood-brain barrier
The vaccine is a live virus that outcompetes the wild strain in nerves
Antibody blocks spread to the central nervous system during the long incubation period
micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.e: Neutralising antibody does not appear naturally until clinical disease is well established, by which time the outcome is fatal.

micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.q: Despite extensive involvement of the brain, histology in rabies shows little beyond:
micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.e: Viral proteins inhibit apoptosis and aspects of interferon action, and little antigen is released, so the infection stays largely hidden.

micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.q: In the United States, rabies is now found more often in cats than dogs because:
micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.e: The dog vaccination programme means sylvatic and bat exposure accounts for most animal rabies there; worldwide the dog remains the principal reservoir.

micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.q: Worldwide rabies deaths are estimated at:
micro-virol-7:rabies-dis.e: Most are children, and at least 20,000 occur in India, where dogs transmit 96% of cases.

micro-virol-7:filo.q: Ebola virus enters cells by binding Niemann-Pick C1 and:
o: Intercellular adhesion molecule-1, which rhinoviruses also use
Sialic acid on surface glycoproteins and glycolipids
T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain 1, also the hepatitis A virus receptor
micro-virol-7:filo.e: Niemann-Pick C1 is a cholesterol transfer protein; replication is in the cytoplasm as in rhabdoviruses.

micro-virol-7:filo.q: Filovirus virions differ from rhabdovirus virions in being:
o: Long filaments 800 to 1400 nm in length
micro-virol-7:filo.e: They may contain no genome, one, or several.

micro-virol-7:filo.q: Specimens from a patient with suspected filovirus infection require:
o: No special handling once the sample is fixed
Level 2 handling with a surgical mask
micro-virol-7:filo.e: RT-PCR of the genome in secretions both confirms the diagnosis and minimises handling of samples.

micro-virol-7:filo.q: The rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine used in the 2018 Democratic Republic of Congo outbreak works by:
o: Expressing the Ebola nucleoprotein in a recombinant poxvirus vector
Supplying monoclonal antibody against the glycoprotein
Delivering whole inactivated Ebola virus with an adjuvant
Making vesicular stomatitis virus express the Ebola glycoprotein instead of its own
micro-virol-7:filo.e: Health workers and contacts around each outbreak were immunised first, an approach called ring vaccination.

micro-virol-7:filo.q: Death occurs in up to what proportion of patients with clinically evident Marburg or Ebola disease?
micro-virol-7:filo.e: The illness begins with headache and myalgia, then nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, then haemorrhage from multiple sites.

micro-virol-7:reo-struct.q: Proteolytic cleavage of the reovirus outer capsid in the gut produces the:
o: Core particle with its enzymes exposed
micro-virol-7:reo-struct.e: Cleavage activates the virus for infection rather than destroying it.

micro-virol-7:reo-struct.q: The double-stranded RNA of a reovirus:
o: Is copied by a host polymerase
micro-virol-7:reo-struct.e: Core enzymes transcribe each negative-sense strand into individual messenger RNAs, which then leave the core.

micro-virol-7:reo-struct.q: The 5'-methyl guanosine cap of messenger RNA was first discovered in:
micro-virol-7:reo-struct.e: It was shown to occur in cellular messenger RNA afterwards.

micro-virol-7:reo-struct.q: Rotavirus VP4 is activated by cleavage into VP5 and VP8, exposing a structure resembling:
o: A bacterial adhesin of the pilus
micro-virol-7:reo-struct.e: Cleaved VP4 lets the virion penetrate the plasma membrane directly.

micro-virol-7:reo-struct.q: Reovirus and rotavirus can generate hybrid viruses in a mixed infection because:
o: The genome is segmented and segments reassort
They integrate into the host chromosome
micro-virol-7:reo-struct.e: This is the same mechanism that produces pandemic influenza strains.

micro-virol-7:reo-struct.q: Reoviruses survive in detergents, over wide pH and temperature ranges, and in aerosols because they:
o: Carry a lipid coat that resists bile
Are non-enveloped with a double-layered protein capsid
Replicate only at 33 degrees in the upper airway
micro-virol-7:reo-struct.e: The outer capsid also protects the core from gastric acid.

micro-virol-7:rota.q: Before vaccination, rotavirus accounted for roughly what share of childhood diarrhoea needing hospital admission for dehydration?
micro-virol-7:rota.e: In underdeveloped countries it caused at least a million deaths a year in undernourished children.

micro-virol-7:rota.q: Rotavirus diarrhoea is described as resembling that of:
micro-virol-7:rota.e: Treatment is supportive rehydration; diagnosis is ELISA for virus in stool.

micro-virol-7:rota.q: The oral live rotavirus vaccine is given at:
micro-virol-7:rota.e: Newer vaccines are safer than the earlier ones and have reduced disease worldwide.

micro-virol-7:rota.q: Colorado tick fever is caused by a member of the Reoviridae and presents as:
o: A dengue-like febrile zoonosis with rash
Acute flaccid paralysis of a limb
Jaundice with black vomit and renal failure
micro-virol-7:rota.e: Orbiviruses and coltiviruses are spread by arthropods and are therefore arboviruses.

micro-virol-7:arbo-cycle.q: Most arbovirus infections are limited to the stage of:
o: Direct invasion of the central nervous system
Local replication at the site of the bite
Primary viraemia, with at most mild systemic disease
micro-virol-7:arbo-cycle.e: Severe systemic disease or encephalitis follows only if enough virus is made during the secondary viraemia to reach critical target tissues.

micro-virol-7:arbo-cycle.q: The flu-like prodrome and the arthritis of arbovirus infection are caused by:
micro-virol-7:arbo-cycle.e: Complement and cell-mediated responses then contribute to the tissue destruction of encephalitis.

micro-virol-7:arbo-cycle.q: Haemorrhagic symptoms in arbovirus disease arise when:
o: Clotting factors are consumed by an anticoagulant in the arthropod vector's saliva
The virus encodes a haemolysin that destroys erythrocytes
Immune complexes and cell-associated antibody activate complement and disrupt vascular cells
Platelets are directly infected and then destroyed
micro-virol-7:arbo-cycle.e: So the disease is a combination of immune and viral pathogenesis.

micro-virol-7:arbo-cycle.q: A disease spread by animals or with an animal reservoir is called a:
micro-virol-7:arbo-cycle.e: Arboviruses have a very broad host range across vertebrates and invertebrates.

micro-virol-7:alpha.q: The alphavirus envelope takes on the shape of the capsid because:
o: The glycoprotein carboxy terminus is anchored in the capsid, shrink-wrapping the envelope
Matrix protein cross-links the capsid and the envelope into one rigid shell
The envelope contains no lipid and so cannot bend
The capsid is flexible and takes the shape of the envelope
micro-virol-7:alpha.e: Two or three glycoproteins associate to form a single spike.

micro-virol-7:alpha.q: Alphaviruses can be grouped and distinguished by antigenic determinants on their:
micro-virol-7:alpha.e: Capsid proteins of all alphaviruses are similar in structure and antigenically cross-reactive, so they cannot separate them.

o: St. Louis and West Nile viruses
Western, eastern and Venezuelan equine encephalitis viruses
Dengue, yellow fever and Japanese encephalitis viruses
micro-virol-7:alpha.e: They are zoonoses with a reservoir in birds and Aedes and Culex mosquitoes as vectors.

o: Much larger with a helical capsid
micro-virol-7:alpha.e: They are 45 to 75 nm; toga is Latin for cloak.

micro-virol-7:rubella.q: Rubella differs from the other togaviruses in that it:
o: Has no envelope around its nucleocapsid
Is a respiratory virus with no readily detectable cytopathologic effect
Is spread by Aedes and Culex mosquitoes
Has a negative-sense genome and carries its own polymerase
micro-virol-7:rubella.e: Humans are its only host and it spreads in respiratory secretions.

micro-virol-7:rubella.q: The fetus is at major risk in maternal rubella until:
micro-virol-7:rubella.e: Maternal immunity from prior exposure or vaccination prevents spread of virus to the fetus.

micro-virol-7:rubella.q: The most common manifestations of congenital rubella are:
o: Cataracts, mental retardation, cardiac abnormalities and deafness
Chorioretinitis and periventricular calcification of the brain
Limb hypoplasia and scarring of the skin
micro-virol-7:rubella.e: Norman McAlister Gregg linked maternal rubella to congenital cataracts in 1941, which prompted the childhood vaccination programme.

micro-virol-7:rubella.q: Since the vaccine era, the commonest infectious cause of congenital defects is:
micro-virol-7:rubella.e: Rubella held that place before vaccination.

micro-virol-7:rubella.q: Rubella virus was first isolated in 1962 by exploiting the fact that its replication:
o: Produces a haemagglutinin on the cell surface
Lyses monkey kidney cells in a distinctive pattern
Forms syncytia in the infected monolayer
Blocks the replication of superinfecting picornaviruses
micro-virol-7:rubella.e: That property is called heterologous interference; rubella is not itself cytolytic.

micro-virol-7:rubella.q: Rubella in an adult, unlike in a child, may include:
micro-virol-7:rubella.e: Rarely there is thrombocytopenia or postinfectious encephalopathy; the rash and joint pain are immune-complex effects.

micro-virol-7:flavi.q: Dengue haemorrhagic fever is worsened by prior infection with another dengue strain because non-neutralising antibody:
o: Causes direct lysis of vascular endothelium
Blocks interferon production by infected cells
Fixes complement onto the surface of the erythrocytes
Enhances uptake of the virus into cells bearing Fc receptors
micro-virol-7:flavi.e: Cross-reactive antibodies are produced between different flaviviruses, so the response to a related strain can exacerbate immunopathogenesis.

o: Eastern and western equine encephalitis viruses
St. Louis, West Nile and Japanese encephalitis viruses
micro-virol-7:flavi.e: The haemorrhagic flaviviruses target vasculature, liver and other organs instead of neurons.

micro-virol-7:flavi.q: Jaundice and black vomit are the classic picture of:
micro-virol-7:flavi.e: An attenuated live vaccine is available for it.

micro-virol-7:flavi.q: Hepatitis C virus belongs to which family?
micro-virol-7:flavi.e: The Flaviviridae include flaviviruses, pestiviruses and the hepaciviruses hepatitis C and G.

micro-virol-7:bunya.q: Bunyaviruses are unique among negative-strand RNA viruses in lacking:
micro-virol-7:bunya.e: The envelope carries G1 and G2 and encloses the L, M and S segments.

micro-virol-7:bunya.q: Bunyaviruses prime messenger RNA synthesis by cap-snatching, but unlike influenza they do it:
micro-virol-7:bunya.e: Virions then assemble by budding into the Golgi rather than at the plasma membrane.

o: The bite of an infected tick
The bite of an infected mosquito
Inhaling aerosols of infected rodent urine
micro-virol-7:bunya.e: Rodents are both reservoir and vector for hantaviruses, unlike the other bunyaviruses, and shed virus in urine for long periods.

o: Disrupting endothelial function so the vasculature leaks, with cytolytic immune destruction of tissue
Direct lysis of the alveolar lining cells
Occluding the pulmonary arterioles with widespread fibrin and platelet microthrombi
Secreting a pore-forming toxin in the lung
micro-virol-7:bunya.e: The virus replicates in the vasculature and kidneys but is not itself cytolytic.

micro-virol-7:bunya.q: Many Bunyaviridae persist in one locality year after year because they:
o: Survive the winter in mosquito eggs
micro-virol-7:bunya.e: Humans who enter the vector's environment are usually dead-end hosts.

micro-virol-7:bunya.q: The 1993 Four Corners outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome followed:
o: Contamination of a municipal water supply by rodent urine
A rise in the deer mouse population after unusually heavy rainfall
A lapse in the local mosquito control
micro-virol-7:bunya.e: Viruses of the Sin Nombre subfamily were isolated from victims and from rodents.

micro-virol-7:arena.e: They are medium-sized enveloped viruses with a negative-sense segmented genome that replicate in the cytoplasm.

micro-virol-7:arena.q: Lassa fever virus and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus are both acquired by:
o: The bite of an infected mosquito
Inhaling aerosols from rodent urine or faeces
Spread person to person in respiratory droplets
micro-virol-7:arena.e: Rodent control is the preventive measure; Lassa fever is African while lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus is worldwide.
Lassa fever virus is the arenavirus that causes haemorrhagic fever.

micro-virol-8:retro-class.q: The 1970 discovery by Baltimore and Temin contradicted the central dogma by showing that:
o: DNA can be synthesised without any template strand
A virus can copy RNA into DNA with reverse transcriptase
RNA can be translated into protein without a ribosome
Protein can direct the synthesis of new RNA
micro-virol-8:retro-class.e: The DNA copy is then integrated into the host chromosome and becomes a cellular gene; the work earned Baltimore, Temin and Dulbecco the 1975 Nobel Prize.

micro-virol-8:retro-class.q: The first retrovirus ever isolated was:
o: Human foamy virus of the spumavirus group
Rous sarcoma virus, which causes sarcomas in chickens
Mouse mammary tumour virus of the B type
Human T-cell lymphotropic virus 1 of leukaemia
micro-virol-8:retro-class.e: Like most retroviruses it has a very limited host and species range.

micro-virol-8:retro-class.q: Which subfamily contains the only retroviruses able to immortalise or transform a target cell?
micro-virol-8:retro-class.e: Lentiviruses are slow viruses causing neurologic and immunosuppressive disease; spumaviruses cause a foamy cytopathology but no known clinical disease.

micro-virol-8:retro-class.q: Retrovirus particles are classified as type A, B, C or D according to:
o: The number of glycoprotein spikes they carry
The morphology and position of the nucleocapsid core
The number of accessory genes they encode
The length of their long terminal repeats
micro-virol-8:retro-class.e: Type A particles are immature intracytoplasmic forms that mature into B, C and D particles after budding.

micro-virol-8:retro-class.q: HIV-1 appears to have entered the human population from:
micro-virol-8:retro-class.e: HIV-2, a closely related virus, was isolated later and is prevalent in West Africa.

micro-virol-8:retro-class.q: Approximately how many people worldwide are living with the virus that causes AIDS?
micro-virol-8:retro-class.e: Antiviral drug cocktails have allowed many patients to resume a normal life, although the infection cannot be fully cured.

micro-virol-8:retro-struct.q: The two cellular transfer RNAs inside a retrovirus virion serve as:
o: Primers for reverse transcription of each genome copy
Adaptors that bind the virion to its receptor
micro-virol-8:retro-struct.e: They are base-paired to each of the two identical copies of the genome.

micro-virol-8:retro-struct.q: How many copies of the genome does a retrovirus virion contain?
micro-virol-8:retro-struct.e: They sit inside an electron-dense core together with 10 to 50 copies of reverse transcriptase and integrase.

micro-virol-8:retro-struct.q: The HIV gp160 precursor is cleaved by protease into:
micro-virol-8:retro-struct.e: HTLV-1 cleaves its gp62 into gp46 and p21 instead; both sets form lollipop-like trimer spikes on the virion surface.

micro-virol-8:retro-struct.q: The retroviral envelope is acquired by:
micro-virol-8:retro-struct.e: The virion is roughly spherical and 80 to 120 nm across.

micro-virol-8:retro-genome.q: Which enzymes are encoded by the retroviral pol gene?
micro-virol-8:retro-genome.e: The gag gene gives capsid, matrix and nucleic acid-binding proteins and env gives the glycoproteins.

micro-virol-8:retro-genome.q: Unlike a picornavirus genome, retroviral RNA injected into a cell is not infectious because:
o: The genome lacks a polyA tail at its 3' end
The genome is negative-sense and must first be copied
The genome cannot be exported from the cytoplasm
Reverse transcriptase and integrase from the virion are required
micro-virol-8:retro-genome.e: The genome does resemble messenger RNA, but replication cannot start without the enzymes the virion carries.

micro-virol-8:retro-genome.q: The long terminal repeat sequences at each end of the genome contain:
o: The genes encoding the capsid and matrix proteins
The origin of DNA replication and nothing else
Promoters, enhancers and transcription factor binding sites
The sequences that encode reverse transcriptase
micro-virol-8:retro-genome.e: Oncogenic retroviruses may carry a growth-promoting oncogene as well.

micro-virol-8:retro-genome.q: Complex retroviruses such as HIV and HTLV differ from simple retroviruses in that they:
o: Encode extra virulence proteins needing more splicing
Have segmented genomes that reassort on co-infection
Do not integrate their genome into host DNA
Lack a functional env gene for the glycoproteins
micro-virol-8:retro-genome.e: They also express distinct early and late proteins.

micro-virol-8:rt-step.q: Besides polymerising DNA, reverse transcriptase also acts as a:
o: Ribonuclease H that degrades the RNA genome
Protease that cleaves the gag polyprotein
micro-virol-8:rt-step.e: It makes a complementary negative-strand DNA, degrades the RNA, then synthesises the positive DNA strand.

micro-virol-8:rt-step.q: During synthesis of the provirus, the U3 and U5 sequences are duplicated so that:
o: The provirus becomes a closed circular molecule
The two copies of the genome are joined together
The polyA tail is removed from the transcript
Long terminal repeats are attached to both ends
micro-virol-8:rt-step.e: This creates both the sequences needed for integration and the enhancer and promoter sequences that regulate transcription.

micro-virol-8:rt-step.q: The DNA copy of a retroviral genome is:
o: Shorter by the length of the primer
Half the length of the RNA
micro-virol-8:rt-step.e: Duplication of the terminal sequences adds the long terminal repeats to both ends.

micro-virol-8:rt-step.q: Once made, the provirus integrates into the host chromosome:
o: Randomly, and then behaves as a cellular gene
At one specific site on chromosome 11
Without the help of any viral enzyme
micro-virol-8:rt-step.e: Reverse transcriptase is the major target of antiviral drugs, and integration is a separate drug target.

micro-virol-8:late-phase.q: The integrated provirus is transcribed by:
o: Host RNA polymerase II, like a cellular gene
Host RNA polymerase I in the nucleolus
micro-virol-8:late-phase.e: Because it behaves as a cellular gene, its expression depends on how far the viral DNA is methylated.

micro-virol-8:late-phase.q: Full-length transcripts of the retroviral genome are used:
o: Both as messenger RNA precursor and as new genomes
Only as messenger RNA for gag
Only as templates for reverse transcription
micro-virol-8:late-phase.e: In simple retroviruses the full-length RNA is processed into messenger RNAs carrying gag, gag-pol or env sequences.

micro-virol-8:late-phase.q: How does an oncornavirus differ from HTLV-1 in the way it causes cancer?
o: It transforms cells without integrating at all
It may carry an oncogene and has a short latency
It needs a helper virus to transform a cell
It integrates but never transcribes its genome
