micro-virol-8:late-phase.e: HTLV-1 carries no oncogene and has a long latent period before leukaemia appears.

micro-virol-8:hiv-entry.q: HIV entry requires binding to CD4 and then to:
o: An integrin on the apical epithelial surface
A complement regulatory protein of the host cell
micro-virol-8:hiv-entry.e: Binding to both receptors is the first and major determinant of tissue tropism and host range.

micro-virol-8:hiv-entry.q: Which co-receptor does HIV use when it first infects a person?
micro-virol-8:hiv-entry.e: Later in chronic infection the env gene mutates so that gp120 binds CXCR4, which is expressed mainly on T cells.

micro-virol-8:hiv-entry.q: People who are deficient in CCR5 are:
o: Prone to rapid progression to AIDS
Unable to clear hepatitis B virus
micro-virol-8:hiv-entry.e: The co-receptor is needed by the macrophage-tropic virus that establishes the initial infection.

micro-virol-8:hiv-entry.q: Which HIV glycoprotein mediates fusion of the viral envelope with the cell membrane?
micro-virol-8:hiv-entry.e: Both CCR5 binding and gp41-mediated fusion are targets for antiviral drugs; gp120 performs the receptor binding.

micro-virol-8:hiv-cells.q: Macrophages, dendritic cells, memory T cells and haematopoietic stem cells matter in HIV infection because they:
o: Present viral antigen without being infected
Are persistently infected and act as reservoirs
Kill the virus but cannot clear it
Are the only cells expressing CD4
micro-virol-8:hiv-cells.e: Murray calls this distribution of persistently infected cells the Trojan horse.

micro-virol-8:hiv-cells.q: HIV can remain on the surface of a dendritic cell by binding:
micro-virol-8:hiv-cells.e: A CD4 T cell can then be infected by the cell-bound virus or by cell-to-cell transmission on contact with the dendritic cell.

micro-virol-8:hiv-cells.q: Late in HIV disease the tropism of some virus shifts from M-tropic to T-tropic because:
o: The env gene encoding gp120 mutates
CD4 is lost from T cells
micro-virol-8:hiv-cells.e: The gp120 of the T-tropic virus binds CD4 together with CXCR4 instead of CCR5.

micro-virol-8:hiv-course.q: The initial illness 2 to 4 weeks after HIV infection resembles:
o: Typhoid fever with rose spots on the trunk
Infectious hepatitis with jaundice and dark urine
Acute bacterial meningitis with neck stiffness
micro-virol-8:hiv-course.e: As in Epstein-Barr mononucleosis the symptoms come from T-cell responses to widespread infection of antigen-presenting cells.

micro-virol-8:hiv-course.q: Full-blown AIDS is defined by a CD4 T-cell count below:
micro-virol-8:hiv-course.e: Symptoms begin as the count falls below 500; at the AIDS threshold the viral load is usually above 75,000 copies per millilitre.

micro-virol-8:hiv-course.q: Which viral protein in blood rises as the CD4 count falls and immune function deteriorates?
micro-virol-8:hiv-course.e: Genome quantitation and p24 levels both track the increase in virus.

micro-virol-8:hiv-course.q: The symptoms of acute HIV infection subside after 2 to 3 weeks and are followed by:
o: Spontaneous clearance of the virus from blood
Rapid progression to AIDS dementia complex
micro-virol-8:hiv-course.e: During this period, which may last several years, the virus is replicating in the lymph nodes.

micro-virol-8:hiv-course.q: The diseases that make up AIDS consist mainly of:
o: Bacterial pneumonia and recurrent otitis media
Opportunistic infections, cancers and direct CNS effects
micro-virol-8:hiv-course.e: Most infected people become symptomatic and the overwhelming majority die of the disease without treatment.

micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.q: HIV must be transmitted in body fluids because the virus:
o: Is enveloped and easily inactivated outside the body
Is destroyed by any contact with antibody
Needs a living cell to carry it at all times
micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.e: A long prodromal period, and shedding before identifiable symptoms appear, are what make the epidemic hard to contain.

micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.q: Which group was at risk of HIV through treatment given before 1985?
micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.e: Blood and organ transplant recipients were also at risk before prescreening programmes began.

micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.q: Which is NOT a recognised route of HIV transmission?
o: Transfusion of blood and blood products
Casual household contact such as sharing cutlery
Breast milk from an infected mother
micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.e: Needle sharing, needlestick injury, tattoo needles and intrauterine and peripartum transmission are the other known routes.

micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.q: Current control of HIV relies on antiviral drugs and screening because:
o: The virus has no animal reservoir
micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.e: Antiviral drugs are also used for pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis, and circumcision reduces transmission.

micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.q: The initial screening test for HIV infection is:
o: A combined antigen and antibody ELISA
A p24 antigen test on cerebrospinal fluid
micro-virol-8:hiv-epi.e: Latex agglutination and rapid oral or urine antibody tests are also used for initial screening.

micro-virol-8:htlv.q: The malignant cells of adult T-cell leukaemia and lymphoma are called flower cells because they:
o: Form rosettes around a central histiocyte
Have a petal-like ring of surface villi
micro-virol-8:htlv.e: They are CD4 helper T cells, and the skin lesions resemble those of Sézary syndrome.

micro-virol-8:htlv.q: Adult T-cell leukaemia and lymphoma caused by HTLV-1 is usually:
o: Fatal within a year of diagnosis
micro-virol-8:htlv.e: A combination of zidovudine and interferon-alpha has helped some patients, but no treatment is approved for HTLV-1 infection itself.

micro-virol-8:htlv.q: HTLV-1-associated myelopathy, also called tropical spastic paraparesis, results from:
micro-virol-8:htlv.e: It is a non-oncogenic neurologic disease; HTLV-2 is unlikely to cause leukaemia but may cause the same myelopathy.

micro-virol-8:htlv.q: Routine screening of the blood supply covers HTLV-1 together with:
o: HIV, hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus
Parvovirus B19 and hepatitis A virus
micro-virol-8:htlv.e: Maternal infection of children, however, remains very difficult to control.

micro-virol-8:herv.q: Human endogenous retroviruses make up approximately what share of the human genome?
micro-virol-8:herv.e: They are integrated, transmitted vertically, and may still influence body functions even when they make no virions.

micro-virol-8:herv.q: Most human endogenous retroviruses cannot replicate because:
o: They lack any long terminal repeats
Their receptors are absent from human cells
Deletions or termination codons disable them
micro-virol-8:herv.e: Poor transcription also limits them, and cells express APOBEC proteins that suppress their replication.

micro-virol-8:herv.q: One human endogenous retrovirus is activated by pregnancy and produces syncytin, which:
micro-virol-8:herv.e: Other human endogenous retroviruses are associated with prostate and other cancers, multiple sclerosis and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

micro-virol-8:herv.q: Which cellular proteins suppress the replication of endogenous retroviruses?
micro-virol-8:herv.e: Apolipoprotein B editing catalytic proteins act on the retroviral genome.

boss.case: A 20-year-old university student has 12 hours of fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and a petechial rash on the legs. CSF: neutrophils, low glucose, high protein; Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci.

qs.q: Empiric therapy for bacterial meningitis in a young adult:
qs.e: ± dexamethasone. Add ampicillin for Listeria if > 50 years or immunocompromised.

qs.q: Close contacts should receive prophylaxis with:
qs.e: Single-dose ciprofloxacin or IM ceftriaxone is also used.

qs.q: Vancomycin is added mainly to cover:
qs.e: Penicillin/cephalosporin-resistant pneumococci; altered PBPs confer resistance.

qs.q: A vancomycin infusion reaction (diffuse flushing) is prevented by:
qs.e: Non-IgE histamine release, not an allergy.
